[2026-14439: lines 17601-17830 of 19533, FR page 45115]
 17601  A. Executive Order 12866: Regulatory Review
 17602  
 17603      Executive Orders 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review), and 13563 
 17604  (Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), direct agencies to assess 
 17605  the costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if 
 17606  regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize 
 17607  net benefits. Executive Order 13563 emphasizes the importance of 
 17608  quantifying both costs and benefits, of reducing costs, harmonizing 
 17609  rules, and promoting flexibility. Executive Order 14192 (Unleashing 
 17610  Prosperity Through Deregulation) directs agencies to significantly 
 17611  reduce the private expenditures required to comply with Federal 
 17612  regulations and provides that ``any new incremental costs associated 
 17613  with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset 
 17614  by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior 
 17615  regulations.''
 17616      This rule has been designated a ``significant regulatory action'' 
 17617  that is economically significant under section 3(f)(1) of Executive 
 17618  Order 12866. Accordingly, the rule has been reviewed by the Office of 
 17619  Management and Budget.
 17620      This rule is not an Executive Order 14192 regulatory action because 
 17621  it is being issued with respect to an immigration-related function of 
 17622  the United States. The rule's primary direct purpose is to implement or 
 17623  interpret the immigration laws of the United States (as described in 
 17624  INA 101(a)(17), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(17)) or any other function performed 
 17625  by the U.S. Federal Government with respect to aliens. See OMB 
 17626  Memorandum M-25-20, ``Guidance Implementing Section 3 of Executive 
 17627  Order 14192, titled `Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation' '' 
 17628  (Mar. 26, 2025).
 17629      DHS provides a summary of the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) of 
 17630  the economic impacts below. For the full
 17631  
 17632  [[Page 45116]]
 17633  
 17634  analysis, please see the RIA posted in the docket of this rule on 
 17635  regulations.gov.
 17636      Under the final rule changes, DHS would more frequently have 
 17637  opportunities to review and collect nonimmigrant information, enhancing 
 17638  the Government's oversight and monitoring of these aliens, resulting in 
 17639  costs and benefits. Over a 10-year period of analysis, DHS estimates 
 17640  the final rule would have annualized costs ranging from $443.1 million 
 17641  to $448.6 million (using 3 and 7 percent discount rates, respectively) 
 17642  when considering both U.S. and non-U.S. parties. When considering U.S. 
 17643  parties only, DHS estimates that annualized costs would range from 
 17644  $119.9 million to $125.1 million (using 3 and 7 percent discount rates, 
 17645  respectively).
 17646  Need for the Rule
 17647      The final rule would ensure an effective mechanism for DHS to 
 17648  periodically and directly assess whether these nonimmigrants are 
 17649  complying with the conditions of their classifications and U.S. 
 17650  immigration laws, as well as allow DHS to obtain timely and accurate 
 17651  information about the activities they have engaged in and plan to 
 17652  engage in during their temporary stay in the United States. The 
 17653  opportunity to assess the nonimmigrant status with timely and accurate 
 17654  information allows immigration officers to verify that the 
 17655  nonimmigrants have not obtained any criminal convictions and do not 
 17656  pose a threat to national security. In addition, as F, J, and I 
 17657  nonimmigrants would be admitted for a fixed period of admission under 
 17658  the final rule, they would generally begin to accrue unlawful presence 
 17659  following the expiration of their authorized period of admission, as 
 17660  noted on the Form I-94 (Arrival/Departure Record issued at the POE, and 
 17661  could potentially become inadmissible based on that accrual of unlawful 
 17662  presence under INA section 212(a)(9)(B) and (C), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(9)(B) 
 17663  and (C), upon departing the United States. These grounds of 
 17664  inadmissibility have important and far-reaching implications on an 
 17665  alien's future eligibility for a nonimmigrant or immigrant visa, 
 17666  admission to the United States, or adjustment of status to that of a 
 17667  lawful permanent resident. Therefore, these regulatory changes may 
 17668  deter F, J, and I nonimmigrants from failing to maintain status and 
 17669  deter them from engaging in fraud and abuse. By increasing DHS 
 17670  assessments and clarifying when unlawful presence accrual begins, the 
 17671  final rule would strengthen the integrity of these nonimmigrant 
 17672  classifications.
 17673  Affected Population
 17674      The final rule would impact F, J, and I nonimmigrants, DSOs and ROs 
 17675  from SEVP-certified schools and exchange visitor sponsors that run a 
 17676  SEVP- or DoS-designated program and foreign media representatives. 
 17677  Overall, approximately 2.1 million persons participated annually in the 
 17678  F, J, and I nonimmigrant programs combined. DHS estimated the 3-year 
 17679  average active nonimmigrants based on data from fiscal years 2022 to 
 17680  2024. Active nonimmigrants are those present in the United States with 
 17681  a valid visa. Over the 3-year period, there were approximately 1.6 
 17682  million F nonimmigrants, 504,000 J nonimmigrants, and 24,000 I 
 17683  nonimmigrants active per year.
 17684      The number of nonimmigrant EOS requests under the proposed rule 
 17685  depends on the unique circumstances of each nonimmigrant visa holder. 
 17686  For example, in situations when the nonimmigrant intends to extend 
 17687  their stay in the United States in furtherance of their academic 
 17688  training and following the proposed regulatory criteria for their visa 
 17689  and program, they would be expected to file an EOS. Therefore, DHS 
 17690  estimates the number of EOS requests over the 10-year analysis period 
 17691  based on the historical nonimmigrant data and criteria from the 
 17692  proposed regulatory provisions. Further, DHS accounts for the proposed 
 17693  transition period in the estimated number of EOS requests. DHS utilized 
 17694  event-based data to have more accurate estimations of the probability 
 17695  that nonimmigrants would take certain actions that require an EOS 
 17696  request. This allowed DHS to estimate the number of EOS requests based 
 17697  on how nonimmigrants act during their stay. Based on the historical 
 17698  data, regulatory criteria, and the transition period assumptions, DHS 
 17699  estimates an annual average of 393,500; 28,000; 6,000 EOS requests for 
 17700  F, J, and I nonimmigrants, respectively, over the ten-year period of 
 17701  analysis.
 17702  Costs
 17703      DHS recognizes that the final rule would incur costs. Some of the 
 17704  costs have been quantified based on available data, and the remaining 
 17705  costs are qualitative.
 17706  Quantitative Costs
 17707      Depending on each nonimmigrant's need to extend his or her stay in 
 17708  the United States, nonimmigrants on an F-1, F-2, J-1, J-2 and I visa 
 17709  would incur costs to request an EOS. The cost burden includes 
 17710  application fees and time for filing Form I-539 or I-539A. DHS assumes 
 17711  a percentage of nonimmigrants would incur costs for additional help 
 17712  filing their request for EOS. DHS estimates the annualized EOS costs 
 17713  for the nonimmigrants would range from $317.9 million to $317.3 million 
 17714  (using 3 and 7 percent discount rates, respectively).
 17715      DHS also calculated a familiarization cost for nonimmigrants 
 17716  expected to be in the country when the rule goes into effect. This 1 
 17717  hour of burden, which is an advising burden to meet with their DSOs and 
 17718  ROs, resulted in an additional year 1 cost of $45.6 million to $43.9 
 17719  million (using 3 and 7 percent discount rates, respectively).
 17720      Further, DSOs and ROs would incur a burden for assisting additional 
 17721  EOS requests resulting from this final rule. When a nonimmigrant is or 
 17722  would be employed under OPT or CPT, DHS assumes HR staff would incur 
 17723  burden per EOS request to track form updates and avoid inadvertent 
 17724  unauthorized employment due to form discrepancies with the Form I-9. 
 17725  DHS estimates the annualized EOS costs for the DSOs and ROs, and HR 
 17726  staff would range from $88.5 million to $88.3 million (using 3 and 7 
 17727  percent discount rates, respectively).
 17728      Additionally, DHS assumes DSOs and ROs would incur costs to 
 17729  familiarize themselves with the rule and to create and modify training 
 17730  materials, and other adaptations such as system wide briefings, 
 17731  systemic changes, and advising of current nonimmigrants of the rule 
 17732  changes. For the final rule, DHS updated the familiarization costs to 
 17733  135 hours per DSO and RO based on public comments received. DHS also 
 17734  added 1 hour of advising burden to DSO, ROs and current nonimmigrants 
 17735  subject to this rule to account for the transition between the old and 
 17736  new rule. The 1 hour advising burden to nonimmigrants resulted in an 
 17737  additional cost of $45.6 million to $43.9 million (using 3 and 7 
 17738  percent discount rates, respectively). DHS estimates the 
 17739  familiarization and adaptation and advising costs in year 1 to DSOs and 
 17740  ROs would range from $267.9 million to $257.8 million (using 3 and 7 
 17741  percent discount rates, respectively).
 17742  Qualitative Costs
 17743      DHS acknowledges there could be other costs that the Department was 
 17744  not able to quantify and discusses these in the following section. 
 17745  Generally, DHS lacked data and information to quantify the qualitative 
 17746  costs below.
 17747  Federal Government Costs
 17748      DHS acknowledges there will be implementation and operational costs 
 17749  to the government associated with
 17750  
 17751  [[Page 45117]]
 17752  
 17753  assessing aliens at the POE for purposes of authorizing an admission 
 17754  period of up to 4 years. CBP officers will need training on new systems 
 17755  and procedures for conducting inspections at the POE consistent with 
 17756  the final requirements on setting a period of admission for F, J, or I 
 17757  nonimmigrants. DHS also acknowledges that there could be additional 
 17758  costs to the government to upgrade SEVIS and provide additional support 
 17759  services to implement the final rule. DHS anticipates there may be 
 17760  costs for SEVIS development, supplemental Federal staff to assist in 
 17761  the development, increased call center volume, and operation and 
 17762  maintenance of SEVIS databases and other DHS IT systems. DHS 
 17763  acknowledges that this rule will require efforts to update systems and 
 17764  train officers. However, these system updates will not incur additional 
 17765  costs, as the updates for SEVIS are part of regular software updates 
 17766  and incorporated within the budget allocations into current financial 
 17767  and resource allocations for SEVIS operations and maintenance. 
 17768  Furthermore, ADIS does not require any additional costs for new 
 17769  software updates as a direct result of the D/S rule. Training costs are 
 17770  similarly expected and incorporated within the overall training budget 
 17771  allocations and incur no additional cost to the U.S. taxpayer. The 
 17772  training for compliance with the rule will be part of regular training 
 17773  and training budgets and cannot be separated as a distinct cost.
 17774  Costs to Schools and Enrollments
 17775      The global market for nonimmigrant students is competitive and many 
 17776  U.S. schools hold an advantage over foreign institutions due to the 
 17777  quality of the programs they offer, however the final rule may have an 
 17778  impact on nonimmigrant student enrollment. The final rule affects only 
 17779  those F-1 and J-1 nonimmigrants who need additional time to complete 
 17780  their program or who wish to continue their education; however, DHS 
 17781  maintains that eligible students should have no difficulty with getting 
 17782  their EOS requests approved, which should alleviate concerns about the 
 17783  uncertainty of EOS approval. Schools may also incur costs for changes 
 17784  to their information systems and practices to implement processing 
 17785  under the proposed rule.
 17786      DHS expects this final rule will affect relatively few English 
 17787  language programs; the majority of ELT students were enrolled in 
 17788  programs shorter than 2 years. Some schools may choose to change their 
 17789  curriculum to be covered in a 2-year time period. It is possible that 
 17790  some language training programs would experience reduced enrollment due 
 17791  to the final rule.
 17792      DHS does not intend for the rule to have a significant impact on 
 17793  participation of other J exchange visitors or I foreign information 
 17794  media representatives. Equivalent U.S.-based exchange visitor programs 
 17795  (outside of academia) may be more difficult to find in other countries, 
 17796  providing less of an incentive for nonimmigrants to choose an 
 17797  alternative.
 17798  Benefits
 17799      DHS expects this final rule to have qualitative benefits for 
 17800  national security by providing DHS additional opportunities to evaluate 
 17801  whether F, J, and I nonimmigrants are complying with their status 
 17802  requirements, or if they present a national security concern. It would 
 17803  deter fraud and abuse of the F, J, and I visa classifications, as 
 17804  requiring EOS requests at frequent intervals allow DHS to review the 
 17805  standing of the nonimmigrant. DHS would be able to enforce the unlawful 
 17806  presence provisions of the INA for those who are not complying with the 
 17807  terms of their visa status.
 17808  Accounting Statement
 17809      DHS has prepared a full analysis according to E.O. 12866 and E.O. 
 17810  13563, which can be found in the docket for this rulemaking or by 
 17811  searching for RIN 1653-AA95 on www.regulations.gov. Table 1 presents 
 17812  the accounting statement as required by Circular A-4 for total impacts 
 17813  of the rule. The proposed rule would have a quantified annualized cost 
 17814  ranging from $443.1 million to $448.6 million (with 3- and 7-percent 
 17815  discount rates, respectively) when considering U.S. and non-U.S. 
 17816  parties. When considering U.S. parties only, annual costs would range 
 17817  from $119.9 million to $125.1 million (with 3- and 7-percent discount

**Locating fee estimates**

I’m trying to identify the exact filing-fee language in the final rule, especially around Form I-539 and the burden-cost tables. The surrounding material mentions an estimate based on a three-month period, but I’m not yet sure whether the rule itself states a dollar amount or refers to an underlying regulatory impact analysis.

I’m checking later sections for cost tables and searching for references to USCIS’s current fee and paper filing, since the fee may appear outside the main rule text.

**Clarifying fee and timing claims**

I’m distinguishing between figures stated by a commenter and amounts officially established by DHS. The final rule does not set one universal individual fee in its regulatory text; instead, applicants should follow the applicable fee-form instructions. The commenter’s estimate of $1,680 for four extensions should not be presented as an official DHS figure, since DHS points to the broader analysis in Table 16. For processing, I can state that the preamble projects 80% of relevant applications being completed within three months, while noting that this is an estimate rather than a guarantee.

summary.text:
**Calculating transition dates**

I’m distinguishing estimates from guarantees: processing 80% of cases within three months is only an expectation, and the approximate cost for four filings is about $1,680.

For the transition dates, I’m applying the later of the EAD expiration or program end, subject to the four-year cap beginning September 15, 2026. Assuming no EAD extends the period, Priya’s program ends May 15, 2027, and adding the 60-day grace period reaches July 14, 2027.**Clarifying transition limits**

I’m separating the ordinary 60-day departure period from the maximum four-year transition cap. For this case, the authorized period runs through July 14, 2027, while the theoretical maximum could extend through November 14, 2030; another category’s comparable endpoint is October 15, 2030.

The master’s program begins August 24, 2027, which falls within five months of the May 15 completion date. That timing appears to satisfy the transfer window, but because the new program extends beyond July 14, an extension of stay may still be necessary.

**Assessing F-1 extension requirements**

I’m determining whether the new program extends beyond the student’s current authorized stay, which ends July 14. Assuming the master’s program’s I-20 end date goes beyond that date, the student likely needs to file Form I-539 to extend F-1 status before the current period expires. Completing one program and beginning a higher-level program can generally preserve status, but the August 24 start date falls after July 14. I’m therefore treating an extension as necessary unless the new program’s authorized dates show otherwise.**Clarifying filing options**

I’m concluding that filing Form I-539 is generally necessary because the new program begins after July 14 and would extend beyond the current authorized period. The filing should be submitted no later than July 14. However, I’m noting an alternative: if the student departs and is lawfully readmitted using the new program’s documentation, an in-country extension may not be required. The answer should therefore distinguish between remaining in the country through a USCIS filing and departing for a new admission.

**Calculating OPT authorization**

I’m determining whether an additional change-of-status filing is required. Because the student files Form I-765 by March 18, 2027, and before the current admission period—including the 60-day grace period—expires, the transition exemption applies. She therefore needs to file only Form I-765, not Form I-539. If approved, her authorized stay extends through 60 days after the EAD period ends: June 13, 2028, plus 60 days, resulting in August 12, 2028.**Assessing readmission effects**

I’m treating the departure and later readmission as changing the student’s admission period from D/S to a fixed period. Using the program end date of May 14, 2027, the authorized period appears to extend through June 13, 2027—30 additional days. Because she departed before filing for post-completion OPT and returned under fixed admission, she must file both Form I-765 and Form I-539. Although the I-765 was filed February 22, the I-539 must be submitted by June 13, 2027.

**Analyzing travel and readmission**

I’m evaluating whether the student needs Form I-539 and how the timing of the Form I-765 filing affects readmission. The key facts are that the application was filed before the program ended and before travel, so the transition provision triggered by departing before filing may not apply.

For travel while the application is pending, I’m considering the post-completion OPT admission rule: readmission may be possible through the DSO-recommended end date on the Form I-20, plus 30 days, if the student carries the Form I-765 receipt notice.**Clarifying admission periods**

I’m applying the new admission provision to a pending post-completion OPT application. Because the application was filed before departure, the rule for students departing before filing does not appear to apply, so Form I-539 should not be required.

The requested OPT end date is June 9, 2028; adding 30 days gives July 9, 2028. I’m identifying the necessary documents as the Form I-765 receipt notice and the latest properly endorsed Form I-20 showing the recommended employment period.

I’m then calculating the separate admission dates for the next scenario.

**Calculating admission and extension rules**

I’m calculating the admission period by adding the program’s expected completion period to the required 30-day departure period. If the program ends on December 18, 2028, the additional 30 days places the admission end date around January 17, 2029—not January 17, 2028.

For the extension issue, an unexpected change in a faculty advisor can qualify as a compelling academic reason when it creates unforeseen research difficulties. Academic probation, suspension, or an ordinary inability to finish would not qualify.

The DSO must update SEVIS before the current I-20 end date; a late request may require reinstatement.**Clarifying deadlines and employment**

I’m confirming that the rule does not set a specific number of days for the DSO to enter the new program end date. The practical deadline is before the existing I-20 end date; afterward, reinstatement may be required.

For the student’s application, filing by the I-94 expiration date preserves the possibility of continued authorized employment while the request is pending. Filing during the 30-day departure period may still be permitted for certain status purposes, but it would not automatically extend employment authorization. The exact filing date therefore matters.

**Clarifying authorized stay**

I’m distinguishing the I-94 end date from the 30-day departure period after completing studies or practical training. Although the I-94 may show January 17, the post-completion period generally permits departure, not continued employment or a new practical-training period. I’m also noting that a timely extension filed during the authorized period can preserve certain student-status benefits while pending, subject to the applicable limits. Because the requested extension concerns continuing the program after its December 18 end date, the key issue is whether filing occurred before completion rather than during the departure period.**Assessing the filing window**

I’m separating two questions: whether the extension request is timely and whether employment may continue while it is pending. A filing received by January 17 could potentially be timely because the authorized period includes the 30-day departure period. However, if it is filed after the program ends on December 18, the student may be limited to continuing the course of study and may not continue or begin practical training or other employment. Filing before December 18 may preserve stronger employment-related protections, subject to the governing requirements.

**Clarifying filing deadlines**

I’m distinguishing the program end date from the additional 30-day grace period. If uninterrupted employment is important, the extension application likely needs to be received before the study program ends on December 18, 2027—not merely before the I-94’s later date of January 17. Filing during the grace period may preserve lawful stay for completing studies but may not authorize employment. A timely filing could continue on-campus employment for up to 240 days, subject to the applicable immigration rules and USCIS requirements.**Calculating employment continuity**

I’m checking the timeline carefully. If the application is filed by December 18, the 240-day employment extension may begin after the I-94 admission end date, January 17, 2028, and potentially run through September 13, 2028. However, a major uncertainty remains: employment may not be permitted during the 30-day post-completion period, creating a possible gap from December 19 through January 17. I need to verify whether the pending-extension rule bridges that gap or starts only after the I-94 end date.

**Clarifying authorization timing**

I’m examining whether the quoted “240 days beginning from the end date of the admission period indicated on the I-94” could permit on-campus work after the program end date, especially when an extension request is pending. The key distinction seems to be whether the request is filed before the student’s program or grace period ends. I’m checking the surrounding discussion for examples addressing employment during the grace period and whether filing before that deadline preserves continuous work authorization while the request is pending.**Interpreting filing deadlines**

I’m reading the provisions together. A timely extension request may preserve authorized stay, while existing on-campus or qualifying economic-hardship employment can be automatically extended for up to 240 days. However, a request filed during the 30-day grace period appears to allow continued study but not continued or newly started employment. That suggests that, to avoid an employment interruption, the request should be received no later than the program end date, rather than during the grace period. I’m checking how the applicable dates interact in the example.

**Calculating filing deadlines**

I’m distinguishing the deadlines for preserving employment from the later grace-period deadline. To keep working without interruption, USCIS must receive the application by December 18, before the program ends. A filing through January 17 may still be timely during the grace period, but employment authorization would not continue automatically, so the applicant cannot work while awaiting approval.

If filed by December 18, employment may continue for up to 240 days after the January 17 I-94 expiration, or until USCIS decides. An approved extension would likely authorize stay through June 18, 2028, including the 30-day departure period.**Assessing travel consequences**

I’m separating the requested extension period from the previously authorized admission period. The additional stay would end June 18, 2028, including the 30-day departure period. If the request is denied after the current admission expires, departure would be required immediately.

For the December 22–January 5 trip, returning before January 17 should preserve the pending application if the traveler seeks only the remaining period of the original admission. However, presenting documentation reflecting the extended program period could cause the pending application to be treated as abandoned.

**Assessing travel documents**

I’m weighing whether admission under a new term could make the pending application appear abandoned. The regulation says the traveler should carry the I-797C receipt notice for the I-539 or I-765, along with an I-20 showing the proposed length of stay; “should” suggests a recommendation rather than an absolute requirement. I’m comparing whether to carry the updated I-20, the prior I-20, or both. The safest documentation appears to include the receipt notice and the current valid I-20, while preserving earlier records for context.**Balancing admission options**

I’m distinguishing admission for the remaining portion of the original authorized period from admission under an updated I-20 extending beyond it. The rule indicates that seeking only the balance does not abandon the pending request, while seeking the later period may raise abandonment concerns. Carrying the receipt notice and both current and earlier I-20 records may document the situation, but the text leaves practical tension unresolved. Admission is not guaranteed, and a pending change-of-status request generally creates separate travel consequences.

summary.text:
**Analyzing transfer eligibility**

I’m examining whether a graduate student may transfer between schools or change educational objectives during the program. The apparent rule is that transfers are generally prohibited unless the student receives an exception for documented, extenuating circumstances. Changing objectives while enrolled in a graduate program may also require an exception.

I’m distinguishing this from progression after completing a master’s degree: starting a PhD at a higher level may be permitted as continued status, while pursuing the same or a lower level after completion may be restricted. The timing and completion of the first academic year also matter.**Resolving transfer provisions**

I’m comparing the timing rules for transferring a SEVIS record with the provisions governing graduate study. The key distinction is whether the student is still in the master’s program or has completed it. During the graduate program, transfer and changes to educational objectives appear restricted unless an exception applies. After completing the master’s, however, transitioning to a higher level may be expressly permitted.

I’m also checking whether transfer eligibility requires maintained status, satisfactory enrollment, no disqualifying history, and timely commencement. The unresolved issue is whether completion ends the graduate-program restriction.

**Evaluating transfer eligibility**

I’m parsing an ambiguity in the rules. One provision appears to prohibit graduate-level F-1 students from transferring at any point during their program, while another excludes someone who is no longer a current graduate student. Since the student completes the master’s before starting the PhD, the transfer may be allowed because it occurs after the original program ends. Other clauses address degree completion, maintaining status, the first academic year, and the five-month limit. The comparison with the related question may clarify which condition controls.**Assessing transfer timing**

I’m comparing two issues: whether a graduate-level transfer is permitted after degree completion, and whether the required timing is met. The five-month window appears satisfied when the new program begins roughly three months after completion. However, the student’s authorized post-completion period may end earlier, creating a separate status problem before the new program starts. I’m also distinguishing the rule’s prohibition on transfers during an ongoing graduate program from transfers made after that program has ended, since that wording may determine the outcome.

**Reviewing status options**

I’m examining whether the student needs an extension of stay before starting the new PhD program. Because the current I-20 ends July 13 while the new program begins August 23, an I-539 may be necessary if the student remains in the country. I’m also checking whether a post-degree school transfer is permitted or whether reentry with a new admission is required. Finally, I’m looking for later Federal Register notices that might delay or modify the relevant provisions, including any implementation suspension through September 2028.**Checking later notices**

I’m checking whether any later Federal Register publication has delayed or suspended the relevant educational provision. My current understanding is that no such later action has been identified, although the existing rule may allow DHS to postpone or suspend implementation through a Federal Register notice until September 14, 2028. I’m treating that possibility separately from an actual published suspension: authority to act does not itself show that DHS has exercised it.

**Interpreting transfer provisions**

I’m reading Q5 as likely allowing a transfer after completing a master’s degree, provided the new PhD is a higher level of study. The “D/S transition group” appears relevant mainly to the end date of the transition stay, not to eligibility itself. The provisions seem to prohibit transfer while the student remains enrolled in the master’s program, while creating an exception after completion. I’m also noting some uncertainty: the exact timing matters, especially the requirement to transfer within five months and satisfy the degree-completion conditions.**Assessing post-completion transfer**

I’m concluding that the SEVIS record can defensibly be transferred after the master’s degree is completed. The five-month window runs from May 14 to October 14, so an August 23 start falls within it. The transfer must occur after completion, not while the student is still enrolled. I’m also checking related requirements: maintaining status, obtaining any needed extension of stay beyond the transition authorization period, and satisfying provisions governing the higher-level program. The final answer should identify every relevant subsection, including transfer, completion, timing, and status-extension rules.

**Evaluating F-1 eligibility**

I’m assessing whether Ahmed can continue in F-1 status after completing his master’s degree on December 11, 2026. Because an MBA is at the same educational level, the rule appears to bar maintaining, obtaining, or being admitted to F-1 status for that new program, including through transfer or departure and reentry. Transition coverage would likely last through the I-20 end date plus 60 days, ending February 9, 2027. An extension filing would not solve the underlying eligibility issue, and an August start may also fall outside the permitted timing window.**Checking timing exceptions**

I’m confirming whether an earlier transfer-out date could make an August start possible. The rule measures five months from the earlier of transfer-out or program completion, so a December 11 completion date still produces a May 11, 2027 deadline; August would be too late. The same-level MBA remains barred through a new admission or reentry. My conclusion could change if DHS formally delays or suspends these provisions, or if the rule changes before August, but I’m not identifying a later notice here.

**Comparing rule changes**

I’m identifying several differences between the proposed and final versions that could affect F-1 students. One key issue is the transition exemption for Form I-765 filings submitted by March 18, 2027, including the final rule’s wording about reserving an extension period. I’m checking whether the proposal used a different six-month deadline and will verify the relevant Federal Register pages before listing at least five concrete changes.**Resolving the deadline**

I’m checking an apparent inconsistency: six months after September 15, 2026, would be March 15, 2027, while the final text expressly states March 18, 2027. I shouldn’t infer the date from a rough “six months” description when the operative language gives a specific deadline. The safest comparison is to report March 18 as the controlling date, note that the summary’s six-month phrasing is imprecise, and verify whether the proposed rule used a different effective date or transition calculation.

**Checking the filing deadline**

I’m revisiting the exemption’s filing deadline because the dates don’t line up. My initial calculation suggested that applications filed within six months of the rule’s effective date would be covered, with March 15, 2027, as the final day. But that appears to be incorrect: the final regulatory text specifies March 18 instead. I’m treating this as a change between the proposal and final rule, possibly involving a revised six-month deadline.**Organizing regulatory changes**

I’m identifying the final rule’s major changes from the proposal and linking each to the relevant regulation. Key points include shortening the program-end grace period from 60 to 30 days, allowing students to begin or resume classes within five months, clarifying graduate-level transfer restrictions, and permitting limited agency delay through September 14, 2028. I’m also including early-completion departure requirements, broader post-completion OPT travel options, departure documentation, and limits on studying during pending extension applications. Finally, I’m separating proposed rules, comment deadlines, and currently effective changes.**Clarifying STEM OPT authorization**

I’m distinguishing two separate concepts: an automatic extension of an employment authorization document’s validity and the independent work authorization available during a qualifying STEM OPT extension. The final rule removes or limits the general EAD-validity extension, but STEM OPT employment authorization is governed separately under 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv). Therefore, STEM OPT employment authorization should not be treated as dependent on the broader EAD automatic-extension framework. I’m keeping that distinction explicit so the final explanation doesn’t incorrectly merge separate rules.

**Clarifying STEM exceptions**

I’m distinguishing the general EAD automatic-extension rule from the separate STEM OPT provision. The final rule may remove automatic extensions for certain renewing EAD categories under 8 CFR 274a.13(d), but it doesn’t necessarily change the STEM-specific work authorization extension in 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv). For Daniel’s pending STEM extension, the key questions are whether he filed timely, whether the STEM OPT EAD was still valid when filed, and whether the transition date affects his filing. I need to verify those details before answering Q10 and Q14(e).**Determining filing consequences**

I’m identifying the required filings and separating status extension from employment authorization. Because the STEM OPT filing occurred after the stated exemption deadline, Daniel must submit both the STEM OPT application and an application to extend status. If the STEM OPT request was timely filed before the EAD expired, the specialized STEM provision should continue employment authorization for up to 180 days while USCIS decides it. I’m checking whether the newer rule changes that provision; so far, it appears to preserve the STEM-specific extension.

**Calculating authorization dates**

I’m calculating the relevant dates carefully. Adding 180 days to June 30, 2027, reaches December 27, 2027. However, I’m also checking whether a later rule changed automatic EAD extensions for renewal filings made after October 30, since STEM OPT may follow a separate provision.

The student appears to hold post-completion STEM-related authorization from July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027. I’m also considering whether authorized stay extends beyond the EAD expiration, potentially to August 29, 2027, depending on the I-20 program-end date and applicable transition rules.**Estimating the stay period**

I’m determining the end date based on the requested 24-month STEM OPT extension. If the existing EAD ends June 30, 2027, the extension would generally run from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2029, assuming approval for the full period.

I’m then adding the applicable 60-day grace period, which would place the potential end of F status on August 29, 2029. The precise result could differ if the extension is approved for different dates or a shorter period, so I’m treating this as the calculation under the stated assumptions.

**Calculating admission and extension dates**

I’m calculating the four-year admission period from the program’s start date, August 23, 2027, rather than the August 2 entry date because that entry occurs within the permitted pre-start window. Four years ends August 23, 2031, followed by the 30-day departure period through September 22, 2031. The spouse’s dependent status generally cannot extend beyond the principal’s authorized stay. If completion requires more time, an extension requires an updated Form I-20, financial evidence, Form I-539, applicable fees, and supporting documentation.**Assessing extension timing**

I’m treating the six-month guidance as encouragement rather than a filing restriction. The application may be filed before expiration when the school issues an updated Form I-20 and the request is supported by a credible reason for additional time. If granted, the extension should cover the period needed to finish the program—through May 14, 2033—plus the 30-day departure period, ending June 13, 2033. The dependent’s authorized stay cannot exceed the principal student’s period, even if an I-94 shows a later date.

**Analyzing status extensions**

I’m separating the issues into dependent filings, status maintenance, and educational-level limits. Lin’s spouse should either be included in Lin’s extension application or file a separate Form I-539; the filing should document the relationship, valid status, funds, biometrics, and fees. A later I-94 could reflect travel or an administrative error, but it would not authorize staying beyond Lin’s valid period.

For the master’s-to-PhD path, I’m checking whether receiving an interim master’s counts as completing a program at that level, which could affect continued F-1 eligibility.**Evaluating degree progression**

I’m focusing on whether an interim master’s degree counts as completing a separate program when the student remains enrolled in the same six-year doctoral program. The key distinction may be between educational levels—master’s versus doctoral—and whether the regulation treats the degree conferral as program completion or merely an intermediate credential.

My tentative view is that continued doctoral enrollment may not automatically violate the rule because the doctoral program itself has not been completed, but the wording is ambiguous enough that the specific school, SEVIS record, and regulatory interpretation need careful verification.

**Interpreting program progression**

I’m parsing whether receiving an interim master’s degree during a doctoral program counts as completing a separate program for status purposes. My best reading is that it does not mean the student has completed the doctorate itself; she remains in the same PhD program. Even if the master’s conferral counts as completing a master’s-level program, the continuing doctoral program is at a higher educational level. The restriction appears to target moving into a program at the same or a lower level, so it likely would not bar continued PhD enrollment.**Applying admission limits**

I’m first preserving the distinction between an interim degree and a separate program: the regulation doesn’t expressly define “award-in-passing,” but its structure supports the view that continuing the PhD isn’t barred because it isn’t a new same- or lower-level program, and doctoral study is higher level.

For the later reentry, I’m reading the four-year limit as running from the program’s start date, not from the latest entry. Thus, although the document lists a 2033 end date, readmission in August 2030 appears limited to the remaining period through roughly September 2031, including the departure allowance. A further extension would require separate filing.

**Interpreting admission limits**

I’m comparing the stated four-year maximum with the scenario involving travel and readmission. The preamble appears to say the limit runs from the program’s start date, so a later readmission would not reset that cap. However, the question’s sixth item seems to assume that CBP could grant a new admission period based on a later I-20 and program-end date. I’m checking whether the regulation measures the period from the program start or from each admission date, since that distinction determines whether the scenario is internally consistent.**Clarifying readmission timing**

I’m examining whether the four-year limit is tied to the program’s start date or to a later admission. The preamble specifically excludes the initial 30-day arrival window from triggering the calculation and instead uses the program start date. That wording may not clearly resolve travel and readmission during the program. I’m therefore distinguishing between an unexpired admission, an expired period, and a new admission after departure, while checking whether a later I-20 can justify a new period without bypassing the overall maximum.

**Evaluating admission duration**

I’m examining whether a later admission could restart the maximum period authorized for a student’s program. The key distinction seems to be between a pending extension of stay, an approved extension, and admission based on a current Form I-20. The governing language may limit admission to the period needed to complete the course, subject to a four-year cap calculated from the program’s start date. I’m unsure whether a later re-entry creates a new independent four-year period or merely preserves the original program-based limit, so the program dates and admission record need careful comparison.**Clarifying readmission limits**

I’m reassessing whether reentry on an updated Form I-20 restarts the four-year admission period. The text allows readmission for the period shown on the I-20, but still imposes a four-year maximum plus the arrival window. It does not expressly say whether a continuing student’s clock resets after travel. Because the preamble ties the calculation to the program start date, my best reading is that it generally does not reset, though the regulation appears ambiguous. Any conclusion should clearly state that uncertainty.

**Clarifying admission limits**

I’m resetting the analysis. If the same program lasts more than four years, an extension is required, so a generalized statement otherwise would be incorrect.

For Q16(d), the August 2030 date falls within four years of the program’s start, while the program ends May 14, 2033. The most defensible reading is that the cap remains tied to the original program start, not reset after travel. The text doesn’t expressly address renewed admission, so I’m noting some uncertainty; an extension is still needed.

For (e), the dependent’s admission cannot exceed the principal’s authorized stay, despite a later I-94 date.**Evaluating EOS coverage**

I’m determining whether dependents must be included when the principal applicant files for an extension. They may be included in the principal filing or submit separate requests; when included through the designated dependent form, the preamble indicates a single fee. I’m also applying the rule that dependent status cannot extend beyond the principal’s authorized period, even if a later admission record shows a later date.

For the congressional-review question, I’m treating the rule as effective September 15, 2026. I’m finding no later notice changing that date, while acknowledging the stated possibility of a subsequent change.

**Clarifying H-1B timing**

I’m distinguishing cap-subject and cap-exempt H-1B cases. The automatic F-1 cap-gap extension generally applies only when a timely, nonfrivolous cap-subject petition requests a qualifying start date in the relevant fiscal year; it extends status and work authorization until the earlier of the approved start date or the specified regulatory cutoff. A cap-exempt employer does not receive this cap-gap benefit. Therefore, if the F-1 period ends before a July 1 cap-exempt H-1B start date, the person may need another lawful-status strategy, such as timely filing for an extension or change of status.**Assessing travel effects**

I’m focusing on what happens when someone travels abroad while a change-of-status application is pending. Under the applicable regulation, USCIS generally treats the change-of-status request as abandoned once the applicant departs the United States. The underlying employment petition may still be adjudicated, but the person would typically need to seek the appropriate visa abroad and request admission in the new classification. I’m also distinguishing the abandoned status-change request from the separate petition, since approval of one does not automatically restore the other.

**Assessing proclamation applicability**

I’m evaluating whether the current presidential payment requirement applies to Lena’s H-1B case. The proclamation appears limited to people outside the United States who must seek admission—such as through consular processing or entry at a port of entry—to implement an approved petition. Because Lena is already in the country and her employer is filing a change-of-status petition, the text likely does not apply to that filing. It could become relevant if she leaves, pursues consular processing, or otherwise needs reentry, unless an exception applies.**Clarifying current restrictions**

I’m distinguishing between an in-country change-of-status petition and a petition for someone abroad. The stated restriction targets H-1B workers outside the United States, while an approved change of status generally does not require entry. If the applicant leaves before approval, the change-of-status request may be abandoned; the petition could instead require consular processing and later admission, potentially triggering the payment.

I’m also identifying the currently effective presidential document, its extension, dates, publication details, and related documents, while checking whether any additional directive affects the restriction.

summary.text:
**Evaluating H-1B fees**

I’m distinguishing between cap-exempt status and fee exemptions, since they aren’t automatically the same. The proposed or final DHS changes may include a $4,000 H-1B fee for covered employers, including certain initial petitions and extensions, but coverage depends on employer size and the proportion of H-1B/L-1 workers. A university’s cap-exempt status alone doesn’t resolve that question. I’m also considering the separate Form I-129 asylum fee, where nonprofit status or a small-employer exception may matter.**Cataloging fee changes**

I’m separating fee increases from newly applicable charges. The 2024 schedule raised the Form I-129 fee to $780, with a $460 rate for qualifying small employers and nonprofits, and added the asylum-program fee: generally $600, $300 for qualifying small employers, and no fee for qualifying nonprofits. A later DHS action applies a $4,000 charge to certain covered employers’ H-1B petitions, including extensions. I’m checking each rule’s scope, effective status, and whether the university qualifies for an exception.

**Clarifying H-1B fee changes**

I’m separating mandatory H-1B petition fees from optional premium processing. The 2024 fee rule expanded coverage but did not necessarily raise the Form I-129 H-1B fee. A proposed 2026 income threshold of $103,265 may affect fee categorization, though I need to confirm its precise role.

The 2025 registration fee and a separate presidential payment are not DHS rulemakings that add ordinary petition fees. However, a 2026 premium-processing adjustment—from $2,805 to approximately $2,965—could apply when expedited processing is requested for an H-1B petition.**Checking fee rulemaking**

I’m reviewing the 2026-00321 document alongside the 2024 fee rule to distinguish proposed, finalized, and merely related changes. I’m also checking whether a 2025 statutory “Visa Integrity” fee belongs in the answer; because it was enacted by statute rather than created through DHS rulemaking, it may fall outside the question’s scope and may not be an H-1B petition fee.

I’m looking for any later USCIS rulemaking implementing that legislation that could affect H-1B filings.

summary.text:
**Researching petition fees**

I’m interpreting Q7c broadly, so I’m checking which fees apply to H-1B petitions in 2026 rather than listing only one charge. The likely core items include the $17,324 and $16,231 amounts, along with the applicable 2024 fee schedule. I’m also verifying the 2026 premium-processing fee for Form I-129, since the question may expect that amount as well. My goal is to provide a complete, precise fee table and clearly distinguish each fee’s purpose.

**Clarifying fee applicability**

I’m determining whether Lena’s petition qualifies for optional premium processing under Form I-907. If she requests it, the additional fee is $2,965; without that request, the premium fee does not apply. I’m treating this 2026 amount as currently in force.

summary.text:
**Checking 2024 fee amounts**

I’m identifying the exact 2024 fees listed under the applicable regulation. For question 7c, I’m planning to include the base filing fee, the asylum surcharge, and the optional premium-processing fee. I also need to account for the fee changes introduced after September 11, ensuring the amounts correspond to the correct version of Form I-129 and the relevant filing category.

summary.text:
**Locating amendment language**

I’m checking the regulatory text for the exact row associated with section 106.2. Searching near the amendment lines should help me identify the relevant entry and avoid relying on a surrounding provision that may not match precisely. Once I locate that wording, I can compare its placement and context with the table to determine whether the row corresponds directly to the cited section.

summary.text:
**Evaluating fee applicability**

I’m distinguishing cap-exempt status from fee exemptions. A university’s cap-exempt classification alone doesn’t determine whether the additional fee applies; I need to know whether it qualifies as a covered employer under the relevant statute.

For the asylum program fee, a Form I-129 filing generally carries a fee, but qualifying small employers may pay a reduced amount and eligible nonprofit organizations may be exempt. A university may qualify for the nonprofit exemption, but that isn’t established merely by calling it cap-exempt. So the conclusion remains conditional on the petitioner’s legal and organizational status.**Clarifying nonprofit status**

I’m noticing that calling a university “cap-exempt” doesn’t establish that it qualifies for the nonprofit exemption. A university may be a qualifying 501(c)(3) educational organization, but that depends on its actual legal status. A public university may instead be a government entity, which raises a separate classification question. I’m therefore keeping the conclusion conditional: I need the institution’s organizational status, not merely its cap-exempt designation, before deciding whether the applicable filing fee is waived.

**Clarifying applicable fees**

I’m distinguishing between cap-exempt status and fee exemptions: a public university may be tax-exempt without necessarily being a 501(c)(3), and cap exemption alone doesn’t eliminate every filing fee.

The optional premium-processing fee is $2,965 from March 1, 2026, for eligible Form I-907 requests tied to H-1B petitions. Lena’s petition would qualify if premium processing is requested, but not otherwise.

I’m also treating the Form I-129 fee—$780, or $460 for small employers and nonprofits—as a baseline filing fee, while separating statutory ACWIA and fraud fees from newer regulatory charges.**Selecting key documents**

I’m treating Q10 as a request for documents beyond the previously discussed H-1B material, focusing on an F-1 student’s transition into post-graduation work. Candidates include documents on H-1B fees, proposed cap-subject charges, employment-related grace periods, presidential directives affecting H-1B pathways, and OPT fees.

I’ll include at least four, identifying each document number, type, publication date, practical effect, and whether it is currently in force. I’m excluding items with little direct relevance, while noting limited relevance where a document could affect a later status transition.

**Evaluating relevant proposals**

I’m separating finalized changes from proposals so the answer doesn’t overstate their effect on F-1 or STEM OPT planning. One finalized item concerns ending automatic EAD-renewal extensions; I need to distinguish general renewal rules from any STEM OPT-specific extension. Another proposal would remove prior-deference practices for certain extension-of-stay and employment-related adjudications, which could affect some F-1 cases but isn’t limited to them. Since the request asks for at least four relevant documents, I’m considering including several carefully labeled items and prioritizing clearly applicable materials.**Checking EAD status**

I’m verifying the EAD rule’s status as of October 14 and focusing on how it could affect OPT-related employment authorization, including the case involving Daniel. The key step is reviewing the final rule’s precise language and any exceptions, rather than assuming the general automatic-renewal change applies uniformly to every category. I’m narrowing the analysis to the relevant provisions so I can explain whether OPT EAD renewals are covered, excluded, or affected only under particular circumstances.

Abstract:
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), proposes to remove 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), which generally provides that USCIS gives deference to a prior approval involving the same facts when adjudicating a request to extend a petition for an alien's employment or stay. This change would better align DHS regulations with the statute, which places the burden of proving eligibility for all immigration benefits on the petitioner, applicant, or beneficiary; strengthen adjudicatory review; and support agency priorities to improve the integrity of the immigration system and better protect the interests of U.S. workers.

Abstract:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposes to remove regulations at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) to restore its previous and long- standing policy of not providing aliens in certain nonimmigrant classifications (and their dependents) with an up to 60-day grace period upon cessation of employment prior to the expiration of the alien's authorized period of stay. This proposal restores a direct relationship between an alien's nonimmigrant status and the specific employment or activity that formed the basis of his or her admission or grant of status in the United States and reduces administrative burden.

**Checking regulatory details**

I’m verifying whether the cited rule preserves the existing provision while leaving the STEM-related language unchanged. The relevant regulation appears to remain governed by an earlier final rule, and the newer rule may explicitly state that it does not alter the current provision.

For the fee question, I’m checking whether the final rule itself provides the applicable extension fee or instead relies on the current filing-fee schedule. I should avoid presenting the $420 figure unless the rule or supporting fee materials clearly establish it.**Clarifying cost and timing**

I’m distinguishing between figures the final rule actually establishes and estimates raised during the rulemaking. The rule does not appear to create a new individual filing fee or guarantee a decision deadline. A commenter’s approximate total for repeated filings should not be presented as the agency’s fee.

The handout can accurately say that applicable filing fees come from current USCIS instructions, while the rule reports that 80% of existing applications were completed within three months. That statistic describes historical processing, not an assurance for every case.

**Estimating filing costs**

I’m distinguishing official figures from commenters’ estimates. The regulatory analysis appears to estimate about $490 in assistance costs for 24.5% of the affected population, but it doesn’t clearly provide an average filing cost in the preamble. One commenter cited $1,680 for four applications, though that isn’t an official government estimate. I’m also checking whether Form I-539 fees should be included; current amounts may be $470 by paper and $420 online, but I shouldn’t present those figures without confirming the applicable source and date.**Verifying fee figures**

I’m separating costs established by the final rule from current filing charges that may come from a separate fee schedule. The final rule may support an estimate involving 80% and $470, but it does not necessarily set the Form I-539 fee itself. A university handout could state the paper and online amounts—possibly $470 and $420—while noting that any biometrics charge must be separately confirmed. I’m checking the applicable fee schedule before presenting those figures as current or authoritative.

  1458  believes that the OPT fees are on par with the educational costs that 
  1459  foreign students incur for one or two years of education in a program 
  1460  of study in the United States. However, DHS acknowledges that there may 
  1461  be instances in which a refund of the payment is necessary when OPT 
  1462  does not proceed as initially intended. The proposed rule includes 
  1463  refund provisions so that educational institutions may seek a refund if 
  1464  the student does not receive an OPT employment authorization document.
  1465  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1466  
  1467      \114\ See Narenji, 617 F.2d at 745.
  1468  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1469  
  1470      The proposed rule intends for schools to pay the applicable fees 
  1471  for eligible students who will engage in a form of OPT, regardless of 
  1472  the manner in which the foreign student obtained F-1 status--whether 
  1473  admitted in F-1 status or through a change of status (COS) within the 
  1474  United States--and irrespective of how the F-1 student obtained an 
  1475  extension of stay when seeking to engage in a form of OPT. In other 
  1476  words, the proposed fee would apply equally for all schools and 
  1477  students seeking to engage in OPT, regardless of whether the F-1 
  1478  student received an Extension of Stay (EOS) authorization through USCIS 
  1479  or through CBP after traveling abroad to obtain a new I-94 to engage in 
  1480  OPT.
  1481      DHS proposes to establish two different OPT fee amounts. DHS 
  1482  believes that the initial OPT fee amount should be higher than the 
  1483  subsequent fee amounts because, when nonimmigrant students initially 
  1484  apply for employment authorization, they may not have been vetted by 
  1485  the U.S. Government since their initial application for an F-1 visa and 
  1486  subsequent admission into the country.\115\ The importance of ensuring 
  1487  integrity in the OPT program is most prevalent at this stage. For the 
  1488  initial fee, DHS also considered the possibility that nonimmigrants 
  1489  could undermine the H-1B visa payment by abusing OPT.\116\ As such, DHS 
  1490  selected a fee amount for OPT comparable to the fee for H-1B visas 
  1491  \117\ that would deter visa fraud. The fee amount is designed to 
  1492  closely align with the H-1B fees to reduce students and employers from 
  1493  using OPT to circumvent the H-1B visa program fees. Schools would have 
  1494  to pay the OPT fee prior to the DSO entering the recommendation for OPT 
  1495  in SEVIS. To be clear, no DSO would be able to enter an OPT 
  1496  recommendation without the school having paid the applicable fee. 
  1497  Through this rule, DHS intends to verify whether the schools have made 
  1498  OPT fee payments for each student that they recommend for OPT,
  1499  
  1500  [[Page 64576]]
  1501  
  1502  thereby strengthening the integrity of the program.
  1503  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1504  
  1505      \115\ DHS recognizes that the application requirements for EOS 
  1506  under 8 CFR 214.1(c) and 214.2(f)(7)(v) may provide DHS with 
  1507  additional opportunities to vet F-1 nonimmigrant students. See 
  1508  ``Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of 
  1509  Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange 
  1510  Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media,'' 91 FR 
  1511  44976 (July 17, 2026). This final rule (hereinafter ``Duration of 
  1512  Status Final Rule'') amended the admission period for F nonimmigrant 
  1513  classification from duration of status to a fixed time period and 
  1514  implemented additional changes to admission and extension 
  1515  requirements. However, not all F-1 nonimmigrant students are 
  1516  required to apply for an EOS to engage OPT, such as those 
  1517  participating in pre-completion OPT or those grandfathered under the 
  1518  Duration of Status Final Rule and subject to the regulations at 8 
  1519  CFR 214.2(m). DHS believes that the regulations currently in effect, 
  1520  together with the proposed OPT fee rule, will provide a 
  1521  comprehensive and holistic approach for DHS to effectively regulate 
  1522  the OPT program.
  1523      \116\ See Proclamation No. 10973, 90 FR (Sept. 19, 2025), 
  1524  Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers.
  1525      \117\ Id.
  1526  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1527  
  1528      Notably, the proposed OPT fees collected under this rule would be 
  1529  deposited in the Treasury of the United States as a miscellaneous 
  1530  receipt pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 3302. ICE would not maintain or use the 
  1531  funding collected under these OPT fee provisions promulgated pursuant 
  1532  to INA 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184, because the statute does not provide 
  1533  legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected. While the OPT 
  1534  fees would be deposited into the Treasury of the United States and not 
  1535  specifically earmarked for ICE SEVP or immigration enforcement 
  1536  activities, the collection of these fees remain essential in addressing 
  1537  the vulnerabilities of the OPT program for the reasons explained in 
  1538  this section. It is also conceivable that funds collected could later 
  1539  be effectively appropriated by Congress to various government agencies 
  1540  to further enhance the integrity of the immigration system. However, 
  1541  the deterrent nature of the OPT fee remains regardless of whether these 
  1542  funds are appropriated by Congress to government agencies for this 
  1543  purpose.
  1544      DHS considered some alternative regulatory approaches to address 
  1545  the issues in OPT that were discussed in sections IV.A. and IV.B. of 
  1546  the rule, such as applying STEM OPT requirements like site visits, 
  1547  training plans, and additional reporting to OPT more generally. 
  1548  However, DHS ultimately determined that proposing a fee for 
  1549  participation in the OPT program would offer an immediate and effective 
  1550  means to strengthen the integrity of OPT with minimal administrative 
  1551  burdens on the government. Unlike more complex regulatory alternatives, 
  1552  such as expanded site visits, increased reporting requirements, 
  1553  additional processes, and stricter procedural mandates, a fee can be 
  1554  implemented quickly and uniformly across all participants. This 
  1555  approach does not require DHS to deploy significant additional 
  1556  resources for enforcement or oversight. Moreover, the effect of a 
  1557  financial commitment is nearly immediate--those seeking to abuse the 
  1558  program are less likely to invest in participation when faced with a 
  1559  tangible cost, making engagement in OPT for nefarious purposes less 
  1560  attractive to bad actors. Furthermore, the financial commitment of this 
  1561  fee may encourage schools to apply a heightened level of scrutiny when 
  1562  reviewing an F-1 nonimmigrant student's request for OPT to ensure that 
  1563  the student is engaging in a legitimate OPT opportunity.
  1564      Although STEM OPT has regulatory safeguards, including reporting 
  1565  obligations, employer site visits, and the Form I-983 training plan 
  1566  requirement, DHS does not believe that simply extending those 
  1567  requirements to the initial period of post-completion OPT would be 
  1568  sufficient as an initial response to the overarching OPT program 
  1569  integrity concerns. Experience with STEM OPT indicates that additional 
  1570  procedural and documentation requirements, while useful, do not 
  1571  eliminate the risk of fraud, abuse, or noncompliance and may require 
  1572  substantial time and resources to implement, monitor, and enforce 
  1573  effectively. Solutions requiring self-attestations, reporting, or 
  1574  reliance on an honor system, without more, are insufficient to ensure 
  1575  the integrity of the OPT program. These mechanisms would need to be 
  1576  paired with enforcement activity, such as conducting more site visits 
  1577  across a broader range of employers, which may function less as a 
  1578  proactive fraud-prevention measure and more as reactive response to 
  1579  violations after they occur. In contrast, by requiring a financial 
  1580  commitment through an OPT fee, DHS would encourage participant to 
  1581  demonstrate a seriousness and genuine intent to comply with program 
  1582  requirements. The fee establishes a tangible stake in the process, 
  1583  helping to distinguish those who are committed to lawful participation 
  1584  from those who may seek to exploit the program. In addition to the 
  1585  current regulatory mechanisms in place, this additional layer of 
  1586  accountability supports the Department's broader efforts to uphold the 
  1587  integrity and effectiveness of the OPT program.
  1588      The Department recognizes the importance of restoring and 
  1589  maintaining public confidence in the OPT program through an immediate, 
  1590  effective regulatory solution, rather than a complex bureaucratic 
  1591  framework that may take years to yield results. By proposing a fee, 
  1592  rather than alternative administrative procedures, the Department seeks 
  1593  to minimize overregulation and complexities while responding to serious 
  1594  program integrity concerns that cannot be addressed quickly through 
  1595  such procedures alone. Recent concerns regarding misuse and fraud and 
  1596  the displacement of American workers have underscored the need for 
  1597  visible, effective action to reinforce the integrity of the program. 
  1598  The fee serves as a clear signal to the public and stakeholders that 
  1599  the Department is taking meaningful steps to safeguard the OPT program, 
  1600  while ensuring that legitimate participants continue to benefit from 
  1601  its opportunities.
  1602      DHS believes the OPT fee is a crucial first step to urgently 
  1603  address fraud, abuse, and noncompliance, in a targeted and immediately 
  1604  implementable manner. This measured approach allows for ongoing 
  1605  evaluation of the fee's impact and effectiveness, providing the agency 
  1606  with valuable data to inform future policy decisions. Importantly, the 
  1607  implementation of a fee should not be interpreted as precluding future 
  1608  changes to the OPT program through additional regulatory requirements; 
  1609  rather, it represents an immediate first step in a graduated strategy 
  1610  to address the urgent program integrity concerns. The Department seeks 
  1611  to retain flexibility to pursue additional regulatory measures in the 
  1612  future should further action be warranted.
  1613      In considering fees, DHS carefully evaluated various fee options, 
  1614  including exemptions to the fee for small educational institutions. See 
  1615  sec. VII.B.6. However, DHS estimates that 56 percent of regulated SEVP-
  1616  certified institutions are small entities. Id. This approach could 
  1617  leave significant fraud vulnerabilities unaddressed, given that many 
  1618  SEVP-certified institutions are small entities. Various factors and 
  1619  data were considered in this proposed rule, as explained in section 
  1620  VII.B.6.
  1621      Separately, DHS acknowledges that OPT is not the only practical 
  1622  training program with the potential for significant fraud and national 
  1623  security issues. Fraud and national security threats in CPT have also 
  1624  been historically prevalent and have increased along with the number of 
  1625  students engaging in CPT. DHS will continue to monitor these concerning 
  1626  trends within the CPT program and will take additional actions as 
  1627  necessary.
  1628  
  1629  D. Technical Edits
  1630  
  1631      The addition of an OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13 would require 
  1632  clarifying that the other fees listed under the current regulations are 
  1633  solely in reference to SEVP fees, as evidenced by the section heading 
  1634  titled ``SEVIS fee for certain F, J, and M nonimmigrants.'' \118\ The 
  1635  proposed rule would add provisions regarding OPT fees under this 
  1636  section, such that it would be necessary to clarify which fees are 
  1637  specific SEVP fees and which are OPT fees.
  1638  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1639  
  1640      \118\ See 8 CFR 214.13 (current) (emphasis added).
  1641  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1642  
  1643  V. Discussion of Changes
  1644  
  1645  A. Establishing a Fee for Initial and Any Subsequent OPT
  1646  
  1647      The proposed rule would establish a fee of $70,000 per F-1 
  1648  nonimmigrant
  1649  
  1650  [[Page 64577]]
  1651  
  1652  student applicable to SEVP-certified schools that recommend an F-1 
  1653  nonimmigrant student to engage in OPT for the first time. See proposed 
  1654  8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii) and 214.13(i)(1). This fee amount would apply to 
  1655  any type of OPT that the student participates in for the first time 
  1656  (irrespective of whether it is pre-completion OPT or post-completion 
  1657  OPT). Id. The initial $70,000 is a one-time fee that an SEVP-certified 
  1658  educational institution must pay for each F-1 nonimmigrant student 
  1659  prior to a DSO's initial recommendation of an F-1 nonimmigrant student 
  1660  to participate in any type of OPT under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii) for the 
  1661  first time. To be clear, this OPT fee would not be tied to a specific 
  1662  employer; rather the OPT fee would be applicable when a school decides 
  1663  to recommend an F-1 nonimmigrant student for any type of OPT.
  1664      The proposed rule would also establish a fee of $30,000 per F-1 
  1665  nonimmigrant student applicable to SEVP-certified schools that make any 
  1666  subsequent OPT recommendation for an F-1 nonimmigrant student who has 
  1667  previously participated in OPT and has previously paid the initial OPT 
  1668  fee of $70,000. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2). As such, this 
  1669  subsequent $30,000 fee would apply to any type of OPT that an F-1 
  1670  nonimmigrant student participates in after having completed their 
  1671  initial OPT (regardless of whether it is another pre-completion OPT, 
  1672  post-completion OPT, or STEM OPT extension). Id. The OPT fee is not 
  1673  triggered by a change in employer but rather a school's decision to 
  1674  recommend a student for any type of OPT. For example, if an F-1 
  1675  nonimmigrant student obtains a DSO recommendation for pre-completion 
  1676  OPT and completes the training, they would need to obtain a subsequent 
  1677  DSO recommendation for post-completion OPT, regardless of whether the 
  1678  employer is the same for post-completion OPT and pre-completion OPT. In 
  1679  this instance, the school would need to pay $70,000 for the student's 
  1680  pre-completion OPT and $30,000 for the student's post-completion OPT. 
  1681  As with the initial OPT fee, the subsequent OPT fee would need to be 
  1682  paid for the F-1 nonimmigrant student prior to the DSO entering the OPT 
  1683  recommendation in SEVIS. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii). 
  1684  Additionally, USCIS would not grant employment authorization to any 
  1685  student prior to payment of the applicable OPT fee for the student. See 
  1686  proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii).
  1687      The proposed rule reiterates that the schools must pay the 
  1688  applicable OPT fees prior to the DSO entering the OPT recommendation 
  1689  for an F-1 nonimmigrant student in SEVIS. See proposed 8 CFR 
  1690  214.2(f)(11)(i)-(ii), 214.13(i). A DSO may not enter the OPT 
  1691  recommendation in SEVIS if the OPT fee has not yet been paid. The 
  1692  proposed rule requires the DSO to confirm that the school has paid the 
  1693  applicable OPT fee prior to updating SEVIS with the DSO's 
  1694  recommendation and before the student can apply to USCIS for employment 
  1695  authorization. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)(B). The DSO would 
  1696  need to provide the F-1 nonimmigrant student with a new I-20 with the 
  1697  DSO's recommendation and OPT fee payment information so that the 
  1698  student may file the Form I-765 with USCIS. See proposed 8 CFR 
  1699  214.2(f)(11)(i), (ii)(C). The proposed rule provides that USCIS would 
  1700  not grant employment authorization to any student where the school has 
  1701  failed to pay the applicable OPT fee prior to issuing an OPT 
  1702  recommendation or in instances where the school has completely failed 
  1703  to pay the applicable OPT fees. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii).
  1704      For the initial OPT fees, the proposed rule provides that a school 
  1705  may request a refund if the F-1 nonimmigrant student has not received 
  1706  an employment authorization document for OPT for which the payment has 
  1707  been made. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1). The proposed rule makes 
  1708  clear that this fee would not be refunded under any circumstances once 
  1709  the F-1 nonimmigrant student has received an employment authorization 
  1710  document for OPT. Id. Similarly, for subsequent OPT fees, the proposed 
  1711  rule provides that a school may request refund if the student has not 
  1712  received an employment authorization document for OPT or an OPT 
  1713  extension. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2). The DSO would need to 
  1714  remove the F-1 nonimmigrant student's OPT recommendation in SEVIS 
  1715  before requesting a refund. For all refund requests, SEVP would review 
  1716  each request on a case-by-case basis and exercise discretion in 
  1717  adjudicating the request. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(2). The 
  1718  proposed rule also provides that SEVP may consider providing further 
  1719  guidance on its website regarding the refund request adjudication. Id. 
  1720  SEVP's determination on the refund request would be final and not 
  1721  appealable. Id.
  1722      DHS has also considered, as an alternative to the approach 
  1723  described above, having the one-time initial fee of $70,000 apply again 
  1724  to any initial period of OPT following the F-1 student's change to a 
  1725  higher educational level (e.g., to a post-bachelor's degree OPT and 
  1726  again to the student's master's degree OPT). DHS welcomes public 
  1727  comments on the rule in its entirety but especially encourages input 
  1728  from the public on this potential alternative.
